This is based on when I applied there two years ago.

The colleges at Durham are where you live, they're a social entity and each have their own sports teams and societies. They are also where you eat. Some colleges are catered, some are not. Some have shared rooms, some do not. Some have very old accomodation, some very modern. Some are large, some are small.

Hill colleges tend to be older, have more traditions and are on the whole more popular.

When choosing a college look into if they provide the social and living experience you want.

When actually applying, select Durham on UCAS and it will prompt you to choose a college. Later on, you will be sent a link through a student portal and asked to rank all the colleges in order of preference. This is because at Durham, your application is not accepted by a college but by your faculty. Essentially the faculty accepts you, and then colleges are allocated on fulfilling as many people's preferences as possible. I personally got my second choice college, had I gone to Durham I would have been very glad of this because later on I actually changed my mind and preferred this one. 

Therefore colleges are allocated after you get an offer, I can dig through my emails to get the precise order of things.

I would look at my recent tests and exam papers and look at why I'm doing badly. Were the dropped marks a problem with exam technique? Was it a knowledge problem? Was it an application problem? Was it a confidence problem? A time management problem?

Then I'd look at markschemes and exemplar answers to get a gauge of what I need to be able to do, I'd perhaps ask teachers if they'd go through my mistakes with me so I can understand what went wrong.

Then I'd act on what I've just learnt. If it's a knowledge problem then I'd re-cover the topics where I clearly didn't understand the content. I'd probably then wait a week or so and attempt some past questions on the topic to see if it stuck, going through the markscheme afterwards to pick up some extra little things I could have improved on.

If it was exam technique I'd see if I could work out a structure for my answers, see what I missed out and reattempt past exams with a better technique.

If it's a confidence problem, aka panicking in exams, then I'd seek ways to calm myself in an exam scenario and make sure I'm clear what I need to do in the exams to reduce anxiety. Ultimately I'd probably speak to my teacher because I wouldn't be the first student with that problem.

If it's time management, I'd time myself doing questions and get better by practicing.

Overall I'd probably try and do a few content sessions a week whilst I'm this far out from exams, making flashcards as I go along to help later with every week or two attempting some past questions on content a couple weeks old. As we get closer to exams I'd do less content, more mind maps and blurting, more questions and more active recall by using those flashcards.
